items.title: The Windrush passengers were British subjects, not foreign immigrants
items.claim: On 22 June 1948 the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 passengers from the Caribbean. Their legal status?

options.text: They required visas and work permits
They were British subjects with full right of entry — the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status, passed weeks after Windrush
They were refugees with temporary leave
They were on military service tickets only

items.reveal:
The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July 1948) defined 'Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies' alongside Commonwealth citizenship. Caribbean people were British subjects; the journey required no permit.

The 1971 Immigration Act removed automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. People who had arrived as children before 1973 should have had right to remain, but the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010 — leading to the Windrush scandal of 2018, when long-resident citizens were detained, deported or denied healthcare.

The Windrush brought around 1,000 passengers total, including Jamaicans returning from RAF service.
items.why: Right of abode in Britain has been redefined repeatedly. The 1948-1973 period when Commonwealth citizens had unrestricted entry is bracketed by very different regimes — and the 2018 scandal shows what happens when administrative memory fails.

items.title: The Luddites were skilled workers protecting trade standards

options.text: Anti-technology mystics who rejected all machinery
Skilled textile workers — stocking knitters, croppers, weavers — who smashed specific machines being used to produce low-quality goods by unapprenticed labour, often after pay cuts and food shortages

items.reveal:
The Luddites took their name from the mythical Ned Ludd. Their grievances were specific: wide stocking frames produced cut-up goods sold as stockings; gig-mills and shearing frames replaced cropping; manufacturers were ignoring the Statute of Artificers (1563) requiring seven-year apprenticeships.

The Frame-Breaking Act (1812) made machine-breaking a capital offence — Byron made his maiden speech in the Lords opposing it. 17 Luddites were hanged at York in January 1813. The historian E. P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) rehabilitated them as political actors.
items.why: 'Luddite' as an insult against anyone who dislikes new technology obscures the actual movement. They were skilled tradesmen defending wages and standards against unregulated mechanisation — not opponents of machinery in principle.

items.title: Children under 10 worked underground in British coal mines until 1842
items.claim: What did the Mines Act of 1842 prohibit?

options.text: All child labour in the UK
Underground employment for women and girls, and for boys under 10 — following Lord Ashley's (later Shaftesbury) commission report with illustrations of children pulling coal trucks
Coal mining itself, switching the country to oil

items.reveal:
The 1842 Royal Commission report on children in mines included engravings of half-naked children — boys as young as 5 acting as 'trappers' opening ventilation doors, girls and women hauling coal in chains. The illustrations shocked Parliament.

The Act banned women and girls underground entirely and boys under 10. Earlier factory legislation (1819, 1833, 1844) limited child working hours and required schooling. Robert Owen's New Lanark mills (from 1800) had already shown a different model.
items.why: 'Reform' was driven partly by humanitarian shock and partly by middle-class anxiety about working-class women. The Acts solved one problem (underground child labour) without addressing others (above-ground work continued for decades).
